title: David Nye on Staying Curious Through Every Wave of Technology
html:
When David Nye was eight years old, he did what many future technologists do: he broke a computer. The difference was that he was expected to fix it.

What began as childhood curiosity became a lifelong pattern—break things, understand them, learn how they work, and build them back better. Long before cloud computing, ERP transformations, architecture leadership and conference stages, David was simply fascinated by what technology could do.

That curiosity would eventually take him from help desks and desktop support roles to some of Australia's largest SAP implementations, a decade at Accenture, and ultimately AWS during one of the most significant technology shifts of our time.

Yet as David reflects on his journey, the story isn't really about titles or promotions. It's about patience, people, and staying curious enough to keep learning when the next wave arrives.

From IT Support to ERP

Like many people in the ERP community, David didn't begin with a carefully mapped-out career plan. After studying Computer Science at university, he worked across a range of IT roles, including service support, system administration and desktop fleet management. It was valuable experience, but it wasn't until he joined a global ERP consolidation project for a mining company that something clicked.

"I was brought in there as a junior doing LSMW conversions with an SAP migration," he recalls. What immediately captured his attention wasn't just the technology itself, but the scale and significance of the systems.

"What attracted me was how complicated these systems were and how important they were to the companies that we're implementing them for."

The experience left such an impression that David returned to university to undertake postgraduate ERP studies. Looking back, it was one of those moments that quietly changed the direction of his career. What started as a technical assignment became a genuine passion for enterprise technology and the complex business challenges it helps solve.

Learning Confidence Along the Way

Today, David is recognised as an architecture leader, cloud specialist and respected community voice. But confidence wasn't something that appeared overnight. In fact, he openly admits that imposter syndrome still surfaces from time to time.

"I think it's honest that everybody feels like an imposter sometimes in some situations."

Early in his consulting career, David found himself working on large, complex programs surrounded by highly experienced professionals. The challenge wasn't simply solving technical problems; it was learning how to navigate uncertainty, ask better questions and build the confidence to contribute in rooms full of experts.

Over time, he learned that technical knowledge alone wasn't enough. Success often depended on knowing where to find help and having the confidence to ask for it.

"It definitely took a while to build the confidence and it took a while to build that right support network around you."

That lesson would become increasingly important throughout his career. Looking back on years of demanding projects, travel and tight deadlines, David believes many professionals make the mistake of trying to carry every challenge themselves. His advice today is simple: don't.

"I've seen too many people and too many colleagues go through hard times where I think if you share that problem, you'll get support."

The willingness to ask for help, rather than internalise pressure, has become one of the defining principles of how he leads and mentors others.

The Move That Reignited His Curiosity

After spending ten years at Accenture, David faced one of the biggest decisions of his professional life. Leaving wasn't easy. The organisation had played a significant role in his development, and many of the relationships he built there remain important today.

"It was a really hard decision to leave a place that you've been for 10 years."

Yet an opportunity emerged that aligned perfectly with the same curiosity that first drew him to computers as a child. Joining AWS wasn't about chasing a title. It was about getting closer to the technology itself and understanding how the future was being built.

"I had an opportunity present itself to me. It was very much being a technologist."

At AWS, David found himself immersed in an organisation driven by innovation. First, he experienced the continued evolution of cloud computing from the inside. Now, he finds himself at the centre of another transformational shift.

"Now I'm lucky enough to be here during the AI wave as well. It feels like I'm at ground zero."

For someone who has always been fascinated by how technology works, there are few places more exciting to be.

Finding His Voice

Although many people know David through conference stages and community events today, public speaking wasn't something he naturally gravitated towards. Like many skills, it developed gradually.

The journey began during university, where he worked as a tutor while completing his honours degree. Later came opportunities to present internally, share knowledge with colleagues and contribute at industry events. Over time, those experiences snowballed into something much bigger.

"I do really enjoy getting up in front of a group and telling a story and sharing some of my knowledge and my expertise."

That doesn't mean the nerves have disappeared.

"There are definitely butterflies there."

For David, public speaking isn't about being fearless. It's about being willing to start before you feel completely ready. That's why he encourages others to begin small, share their experiences and look for opportunities to contribute.

Today, through SAP Inside Track Melbourne, he actively helps create those opportunities for the next generation of speakers and community contributors.

The Lessons Hidden Inside Pressure

Anyone who has worked on ERP programs knows they can be intense. Long hours, travel, high expectations and critical deadlines often come with the territory. David has experienced all of it.

He recalls projects involving fourteen-hour days, difficult cutovers and one particularly memorable disaster recovery event where he remained awake for almost forty hours while helping bring a production system back online. At the time, those moments felt overwhelming. Looking back, they became some of the most valuable lessons of his career.

"I think everything's solvable. You just need to sit down and look at your options and map out the best possible way forward."

Those experiences taught him the importance of maintaining a clear head under pressure, involving others in difficult decisions and resisting the temptation to panic when challenges arise. Often, the path forward becomes visible only when you pause long enough to assess the situation properly.

Redefining Success

Like many ambitious professionals, David once measured success by promotions, titles and career progression. Early in his career, the next role always seemed like the most important destination.

Over time, that perspective changed.

Today, success is less about climbing the ladder and more about the quality of the people around him, the relationships he builds and the problems he gets to solve. Rather than focusing solely on the next promotion, he finds greater fulfilment in meaningful work and strong professional networks.

"I'm more interested in building the right network both within and outside my organisation."

It's a subtle shift, but an important one. The ladder still exists, but it is no longer the sole measure of achievement.

Riding the AI Wave

When the conversation turns to the future, one topic consistently captures David's attention: artificial intelligence.

Not because it's the latest trend, but because he believes it will fundamentally change the way people work across industries. In his view, we're only at the beginning of what AI will eventually become.

"We're really just right at the start of the AI wave."

His advice for anyone entering ERP or technology today is to get involved early. Experiment. Explore. Learn by doing. The biggest opportunities won't come from simply automating existing processes; they'll come from entirely new ways of solving problems.

"It's not about doing what I did yesterday, today, but with AI. It's about doing things that you never thought about doing before."

For someone who has spent a lifetime embracing new technology, AI feels less like a disruption and more like the next great adventure.

A Marathon, Not a Sprint

Towards the end of our conversation, David was asked what advice he would give his younger self. His answer was immediate.

"Be patient."

It's a lesson earned through decades of experience, career pivots, difficult projects and constant technological change. Looking back, he realises many of the things he once rushed towards would have arrived in time anyway.

Today, he hopes others entering the ERP industry understand that meaningful careers are built gradually. Success doesn't happen overnight, and there is value in enjoying the journey while it unfolds.

If there's one message David hopes people take away from his story, it's this: stay curious, keep learning, ask for help when you need it, and trust the process.

Because in technology, as in life, it's rarely a sprint. It's a marathon.

title: Narayan Vishwanathan on Staying Humble, Staying Curious, and Seeing the Human Side of Payroll
html:
Payroll can look simple from the outside. People submit their timesheets. The system runs. Money lands in the right bank account on the right day.

But for Narayan Vishwanathan, payroll has never been just numbers, rules, or compliance. It is people. It is trust. It is late timesheets, changing legislation, different countries, anxious clients, weekend testing, and the quiet pressure of making sure something deeply personal happens correctly.

“It’s like a goalkeeper’s job,” Narayan says. “It’s a very thankless job.”

And yet, after years across India, South Africa, Australia, New Zealand and Singapore, through mining, public sector and health, Narayan still speaks about ERP with curiosity, humility and a genuine respect for the people behind the systems.

Finding His Way Into SAP

Narayan grew up in Mumbai, India, and began his career at Accenture after university. Like many graduates at the time, he entered a world full of technology pathways. Some went into Microsoft technologies. Others into Java.

Narayan found himself in SAP ABAP.

“It was a very new world for me,” he says. At university, he had mostly worked with open-source technologies. SAP felt different — new syntax, new structures, and a bigger question to understand: how does this actually go out into the real world?

Within six months, he moved into HR payroll, working on a global mining company account. It was a fast transition, but one that shaped the rest of his career.

Supported by a strong team, Narayan was able to learn by doing. He worked across SAP time and payroll, supported 13 countries, made mistakes, learned from them, and slowly built the confidence to speak with customers across different cultures and regions.

That early experience, he says, “put that bone in me” as an SAP HR and payroll functional consultant.

The Hidden Complexity of Payroll

For Narayan, one of the biggest misunderstandings about payroll is that people assume it is simple.

“They think it is very simplistic, that you get people paid on a particular day and that’s it. It’s just a build, set and forget system.”

But payroll is rarely still.

Someone submits their timesheet late. A payment needs to be handled off-cycle. Superannuation has not been accounted for yet. A rate is wrong and only discovered months after implementation. A piece of legislation changes, and suddenly the arithmetic inside the system has to catch up with the law.

“It’s where law and arithmetic come together, which doesn’t happen a lot.”

That complexity has kept him learning across countries and industries. Sometimes, lessons from South African payroll could be applied in Singapore or Australia. Each country has its own laws, but the challenges often echo one another.

For Narayan, that constant learning keeps him grounded.

“You always keep learning, and that kind of has the humility built in as well. Because you know that it’s just one error away from being completely slammed.”

Learning to Work Across Cultures

A major turning point came in 2014, when Narayan moved to South Africa. It was the first time he had lived away from India for more than a year.

The weather was different. The infrastructure was different. The safety concerns were real. He did not even know how to drive at the time, in a country where driving was almost essential.

But he took the leap.

“Unless I take the leap, I’m never going to know better."

Within a few months, working with people from different backgrounds gave him a lasting confidence. He realised that most people are not trying to make life difficult. They want to get the work done. They want clarity. They want respect.

That experience shaped how he collaborates today: be respectful, stay in your lane, avoid unnecessary tension, and be clear when it is time to talk about the work.

Leadership as Shepherding

As Narayan moved from consultant into lead roles, leadership did not arrive as a sudden title. He was supported into it by the people and ecosystems around him.

That has shaped how he now supports others.

For Narayan, leadership is not about knowing everything in every meeting. It is about knowing when to step back, abstract the discussion, park the right questions, and come back with clarity. It is about enabling people with the right documents, links and context, rather than spoon-feeding every detail.

Most of all, it is about empathy.

When clients are frustrated, Narayan tries to see the bigger picture. Behind the frustration may be investment, effort, testing, weekend work, and the pressure of getting a solution right.

“You’re not only leading your team. You have to lead the client, the customer, to the correct solution.”

He pauses, then adds a word that feels very Narayan.

“It’s like shepherding.”

Grounded, humble, and quietly steady.

The Person Outside the System

Away from work, Narayan is an amateur vocalist. He plays cricket with friends. He is also the father of a three-year-old daughter, which means life outside ERP is full, busy and often delightfully chaotic.

He loves watching films and series from different cultures and languages, and he has a long-standing curiosity about the world. In fact, he says he can still name the capital of every country.

Travel, for Narayan, is not just about landmarks. He wants to understand how people live.

When he visits a place, he pays attention to the ordinary details. What does Singapore feel like on a Wednesday afternoon at lunchtime? What colours appear on the street? What songs are playing on the radio? What local commercials are people hearing?

He is interested in the rhythm of real life, not just the postcard version.

That curiosity also connects to one of his proudest personal achievements: settling in Australia in 2017.

Having family members who had studied or worked overseas, Narayan always carried a quiet desire to travel, experience the world, and build a life abroad. Australia became that place.

Sharing Knowledge Without Fear

For those starting out in ERP, Narayan’s advice is simple: do not be afraid to make mistakes.

He has seen people avoid difficult paths because they are unsure who will support them if they get something wrong. But growth, he believes, comes from trying, learning and being open enough to ask.

He also believes deeply in knowledge sharing.

Some consultants fear that sharing knowledge will reduce their value. Narayan sees the opposite.

“If you’re able to share more, even with the client, it’s not that your job is going to be made redundant in the future,” he says. “They’ll learn more and they’ll keep on asking more questions.”

In other words, generosity expands the work. It builds trust. It brings others along.

A Human-Led Future

As ERP and SuccessFactors move further into the AI era, Narayan is optimistic, but clear-eyed.

He sees AI as useful for taking away menial, repetitive work. He has already used tools like Copilot for Excel analysis, complex pivots, lookups and PowerPoint support.

But he does not believe AI should replace the human layer.

“It has to be in coexistence with humans, and it can’t replace humans."

For Narayan, technology works best when it serves people. And perhaps that is the thread running through his whole story: systems matter, but people matter more.

The payroll must run. The solution must work. The data must be right.

But behind every process is a person waiting to be paid, a team trying to deliver, a client carrying pressure, and a consultant learning to stay humble enough to keep getting better.

title: Vaibhav Tiwari on Why Success Is a Journey, Not a Destination
html:
When we're young, success often feels like a destination. It's the next promotion, the next opportunity, the next milestone waiting somewhere in the distance. But over time, our understanding of success evolves. We begin to realise that growth isn't defined by a single achievement but by the people we help, the lessons we learn, and the impact we create along the way.

For Vaibhav Tiwari, that shift has been shaped by decades of leadership, global transformation programs, and a career spent sitting at the intersection of business and technology. Along the way, he has learned that technology alone never solves problems, leadership is rarely about having all the answers, and the most successful teams are built on trust, honesty, and continuous improvement.

Finding His Way to SAP

Interestingly, Vaibhav's path into ERP wasn't planned from the beginning. He studied Chemical Engineering at one of India's leading engineering institutions before entering the software industry as a developer. Like many graduates of his generation, technology offered exciting career opportunities, and he quickly secured a role through campus recruitment. Yet after spending time in software development, he realised something was missing.

"I realised that perhaps I'm not enjoying being a developer too much."

Rather than continuing down a path that didn't feel right, he stepped back and reassessed. He enrolled in an MBA specialising in Information Management, determined to find a career that combined technology with business. During that time, SAP regularly recruited from his university, and everything he heard about the organisation resonated with him. It offered exposure to technology, business processes, global industries and, importantly, the opportunity to work with people around the world.

Vaibhav didn't leave the opportunity to chance. He deliberately worked towards becoming a strong SAP candidate, completing specialised coursework and even studying German for a year to strengthen his profile. The effort paid off. SAP recruited him into its consulting division, beginning a journey that would shape the rest of his career.

Learning That Technology Isn't the Starting Point

After joining SAP, Vaibhav was sent through extensive training to learn the company's products and consulting methodologies. He soon found himself working within SAP's International Consulting Group, a specialised team responsible for helping customers adopt new products before they were widely available in the market.

The work was challenging and often unpredictable. These were solutions that few people understood, supporting business problems that had rarely been addressed before. Whether working with automotive manufacturers in the United States or supporting Nokia in Finland during its peak years, every project required a willingness to learn, adapt and solve unfamiliar challenges.

Yet the biggest lesson wasn't technical.

"Technology is an enabler to solve a business problem. You should not implement technology just for the sake of technology."

That principle became one of the foundations of his leadership philosophy. Too often, organisations become fascinated by the latest technology without fully understanding the problem they are trying to solve. For Vaibhav, successful transformation begins with clarity around business outcomes. Only then can technology play its role as an enabler.

"It's about solving the right thing and doing it right."

The Coffee Mug That Stayed With Him

Throughout his career, Vaibhav has worked on major transformation programs across industries and countries. While methodologies, technologies and organisations have changed over the years, one simple lesson has stayed with him.

During a project with BHP Billiton in Australia, every team member was given a coffee mug carrying a simple phrase:

"Plan the work and work the plan."

What started as a slogan became a guiding principle. Vaibhav believes successful projects require careful planning, clear objectives and disciplined execution. The more uncertainty a project contains, the more important it becomes to establish clarity around goals, responsibilities and expectations from the very beginning.

Equally important is maintaining transparency with stakeholders. Over the years, he has learned that every person involved in a project defines success differently. A customer may have one vision of success, a project team another, and leadership yet another. The only way to align those perspectives is through honest conversation.

"If you are open and honest, they will also be open and honest with you, and they will share what does a win look like for them."

Once people understand what success looks like for one another, finding a genuine win-win outcome becomes far more achievable.

When Leadership Stops Being About Answers

Like many technical professionals, Vaibhav's early career was built on expertise. His value came from solving problems, providing guidance and delivering answers. However, as his responsibilities expanded and he began leading larger teams and programs, he encountered an important reality.

"I realised that I can't be everywhere. I can't solve all the problems."

That realisation marked a turning point in how he approached leadership. During his time working with Rio Tinto, he recognised that success was no longer about personally solving every issue. Instead, it was about creating the structures, communication channels and decision-making frameworks that enabled others to succeed.

Leadership became less about directing and more about enabling. It meant ensuring information flowed freely throughout teams, encouraging people to raise issues early, and building trust so that concerns weren't hidden until they became larger problems. Most importantly, it meant creating an environment where people believed their feedback mattered.

As Vaibhav points out, people only speak up when they believe something will be done with the information they share. Building that confidence takes consistency, follow-through and genuine care.

Building Teams Around Strengths

One of the themes that appears repeatedly throughout Vaibhav's story is the importance of self-awareness. In his experience, trust doesn't begin with processes or frameworks. It begins with honesty.

For leaders, that means openly acknowledging both strengths and weaknesses.

"Nobody is perfect."

When leaders create that level of openness, team members become more comfortable doing the same. Rather than pretending to be experts in everything, people can focus on the areas where they add the most value. One person may excel at analytics, another at stakeholder engagement, another at communication or problem-solving. The goal isn't to create individuals who are strong at everything. The goal is to build teams whose strengths complement one another.

"How do you achieve that? You achieve that by accepting what are your strengths and what are your weaknesses."

For Vaibhav, high-performing teams are built when people understand what they bring to the table and trust others to contribute their own strengths.

Solving the Problem, Not the Person

When asked how he handles mistakes and failures within teams, Vaibhav returned to a principle that has become central to his leadership approach.

"Solve the problem and not the person."

He believes that when discussions focus on blame, learning stops. People become defensive, information gets hidden, and the real causes of problems remain unresolved. By contrast, when teams focus on understanding the issue itself, individuals are more willing to share what happened, identify gaps and contribute to solutions.

"If you start the direction towards a person, then the problem is never solved."

This doesn't mean accountability disappears. Instead, accountability shifts towards understanding root causes, improving processes and ensuring mistakes aren't repeated. In Vaibhav's view, making mistakes is part of growth. Repeating the same mistakes after learning from them is where the real challenge begins.

Seeing the Bigger Picture

One piece of advice Vaibhav consistently offers younger professionals is to look beyond their immediate responsibilities.

Many people assume their leaders have all the answers. In reality, he believes leadership often involves managing competing priorities, constraints and expectations rather than possessing superior technical knowledge.

"Younger people often think that my boss knows everything. And that is completely untrue."

What leaders often see more clearly is the broader context surrounding a project. They understand the organisational objectives, budget realities, stakeholder expectations and strategic priorities influencing decisions. Professionals who learn to understand that bigger picture early in their careers position themselves to make better decisions and create greater value.

"If you start to think about the value generated out of that particular technology or a problem, you will do a better job."

For Vaibhav, empathy plays a critical role in that process. Understanding how customers, users and stakeholders experience a solution often leads to better outcomes than focusing solely on the technology itself.

Family, Food and Finding Balance

Outside work, Vaibhav's greatest source of support comes from his family. Throughout a career that has taken him across continents and demanded long hours, his wife, children and loved ones have provided the stability that makes everything else possible.

"My wife has supported me tremendously in all my journey."

Like many leaders, finding balance isn't always easy. His current role often requires late-night meetings across multiple time zones, creating a demanding schedule. Yet when he needs to recharge, he gravitates towards simple activities that allow him to focus entirely on the present moment.

Sometimes that means fixing something around the house. Other times, it means cooking.

"I like cooking, so when I'm too stressed, I start to cook something and I create some dish."

In a world filled with constant demands, those small moments of focus provide an opportunity to reset.

Success as a Continuous Journey

Perhaps the most powerful reflection from Vaibhav's story is how his definition of success has evolved over time.

“When I was young, success was a destination. The more experienced I get, the more I see success as a journey.”

Today, success isn't defined by a title, a project or a single achievement. It's measured through continuous improvement, helping teams grow, delivering value to customers and creating environments where people can thrive. Progress doesn't always come through dramatic breakthroughs. More often, it comes through small, consistent improvements repeated over time.

"It's a regular journey of slow improvements, but continuous improvement is how I define success."

That perspective extends beyond his own career. For Vaibhav, growth only becomes meaningful when the people around you are growing too.

Staying Curious in the Age of AI

Despite decades of experience, Vaibhav remains deeply committed to learning. His latest focus is artificial intelligence, an area he finds both exciting and transformative. Rather than relying solely on self-study, he recently enrolled in an online university program to formally deepen his understanding of AI.

"If at my life stage, I can go and join a university program to learn AI and force myself to do coding and give exam, then I think you have to do it."

He believes the next generation of professionals will face a world that changes faster than any previous generation has experienced. The skills people learn today may not perfectly match the challenges they encounter tomorrow. As a result, adaptability and continuous learning will become increasingly important.

His advice is simple: never stop learning.

Technology will continue to evolve. Industries will continue to change. The professionals who thrive will be those willing to evolve alongside them.

A Human-Centred View of Transformation

After decades of leading transformations, Vaibhav still believes the biggest mistake organisations make is assuming technology alone will create change.

Successful transformation requires much more. It requires clear objectives, measurable outcomes, engaged people, effective processes and trusted data. Technology plays an important role, but only when those foundations are already in place.

"Just throwing a technology onto it will not solve the problem."

For someone who has spent his career in ERP and digital transformation, it is a refreshingly human perspective. Because beneath every system, every project and every transformation are people trying to solve real problems and create better outcomes.

And perhaps that's what defines Vaibhav's story best. Not the technologies he has implemented or the programs he has led, but his belief that lasting success comes from helping people grow, work together and continuously improve along the journey.

title: John Hutchinson on Leading with Calm in a World of Complexity
html:
For more than three decades, John Hutchinson has helped organisations navigate some of the world's most complex ERP transformations. He's worked across Australia, Singapore, New Zealand, and now Ireland, leading major SAP programs and guiding teams through change.

Yet when John reflects on his career, what stands out isn't the technology or the scale of the projects. It's the people, the opportunities to learn, and the quiet realisation that leadership doesn't have to be loud to make an impact.

Growing Up Curious

Long before SAP, project plans, and global transformations, John was simply a curious kid fascinated by understanding how things worked. His father was an electronics technician, and many of John's earliest memories involve helping around the house and being exposed to technology in practical ways.

Science and mathematics came naturally at school, and those strengths eventually led him to university, where he completed a Bachelor of Science with majors in Computer Science and Applied Mathematics.

"I was interested in the science aspect of it, how things worked."

At university, John found himself increasingly drawn to computing. What began as just one subject among many quickly became a passion as he achieved strong results and discovered a genuine fascination with the logic behind technology. Looking back, it wasn't just computers that interested him; it was understanding the systems and processes that made everything work.

Finding a Home in Consulting

While John's studies were deeply technical, his professional career soon became centred on people, business, and problem-solving. When he joined IBM, he found himself in consulting, an environment that constantly challenged him to learn new industries, work with different clients, and solve different problems.

What many people see as a remarkable 25-year tenure, John experienced as a series of new opportunities.

"It was almost like changing jobs."

Every few years brought a new project, a new team, and a new challenge. That variety kept him engaged and curious, while IBM's strong project management discipline provided the foundation he needed to grow. The organisation invested heavily in training and methodology, helping him develop the structured approach that would define much of his leadership style.

A Career That Crossed Borders

One of the defining chapters of John's career came when he relocated to Singapore to work on BHP's 1SAP program, which at the time was one of the largest SAP projects in the world. It was an opportunity that combined professional growth with personal adventure, allowing him and his wife to experience life in another country while contributing to a transformation of global significance.

The experience broadened his perspective in ways that went beyond technology. Working alongside people from Asia, Australia, Europe, and North America reinforced the reality that ERP is fundamentally a people business. Different cultures bring different perspectives, and successful projects require leaders who understand and respect those differences.

"You need to be aware of it. You need to acknowledge it."

Whether collaborating with teams in India, New Zealand, Singapore, or Ireland, John learned that trust begins with understanding. Recognising cultural differences, respecting traditions, and setting clear expectations are all part of building high-performing teams across borders.

The Introvert Who Became a Leader

One of the most surprising parts of John's story is that leadership didn't always feel like an obvious fit. Early in his career, he questioned whether project management was the right path. As a self-described introvert, he often received feedback that he needed to be more assertive, and there were moments when he wondered whether he should return to a purely functional consulting role.

But something kept drawing him back to project leadership. He loved bringing people together, coordinating moving parts, and helping teams deliver outcomes that no single workstream could achieve alone. He enjoyed seeing the bigger picture and making sure all the pieces connected.

Over time, he realised that leadership doesn't need to follow a single template.

"A project manager doesn't have to be screaming and demanding all the time."

Instead, John built his leadership style around calmness, clarity, and consistency. The mentors who influenced him throughout his career reinforced that effective leadership isn't about being the loudest voice in the room. It's about staying composed under pressure, setting clear expectations, and creating an environment where people know what success looks like.

Today, those qualities are among the reasons people enjoy working with him.

What Makes a Project Truly Successful?

After decades in ERP, John has developed a clear view of what success looks like. It isn't simply delivering software on time or within budget. Those things matter, but they aren't the ultimate measure.

"It's got to transform the business. It's got to deliver the benefits that it's supposed to."

For John, successful transformation happens when people genuinely embrace new ways of working. It's when business processes become more consistent, teams collaborate more effectively, and organisations realise the value that justified the investment in the first place.

That belief has remained consistent throughout his career. Whether working on OneSAP at BHP or helping organisations navigate large-scale transformations today, his focus has always been on outcomes rather than outputs. Technology is important, but people are what ultimately determine whether a transformation succeeds.

Staying Grounded

ERP projects are demanding. Tight deadlines, competing priorities, and constant problem-solving can easily consume every available hour. Over the years, John has learned that sustaining a long career requires more than technical expertise; it requires perspective.

One of the ways he recharges is through cycling. Time on the bike gives him space to clear his mind, reset, and step away from the pressures of project delivery. More recently, he has also become increasingly intentional about maintaining boundaries between work and life.

"I've learned that there's never enough hours in the day. So you've just got to do the right things that day and then what's not done, pick up the next day."

It's a simple philosophy, but one that reflects the calm pragmatism he brings to both leadership and life.

A New Chapter in Ireland

After more than two decades with IBM, many people might have expected John to stay exactly where he was. Instead, he chose something new.

With Irish family roots and a long-standing desire to work overseas again, he joined Deloitte's SAP practice and relocated to Ireland. The move wasn't driven by ambition or a desire for a bigger title. It was driven by curiosity, adventure, and a desire to experience another part of the world before the next chapter of life begins.

Having previously worked abroad in Singapore, John knew how rewarding those experiences could be. Ireland offered the opportunity to reconnect with family history, build new relationships, and continue learning in a different environment.

For someone who has always valued growth through experience, it felt like the right move at exactly the right time.

Passing On the Wisdom

As John looks ahead, his focus has shifted. Retirement is visible on the horizon, and while he remains deeply engaged in the work, he is increasingly motivated by the opportunity to help others succeed.

After decades of leading projects, navigating transformations, and building global teams, he sees immense value in sharing what he has learned with the next generation. Mentoring younger professionals has become one of the most rewarding aspects of this stage of his career, allowing him to pass on not only technical knowledge but also the lessons that come from managing people, pressure, and change.

At the same time, he remains curious about what's next. The rise of artificial intelligence is reshaping the technology landscape, creating new opportunities and new questions for organisations around the world.

Yet despite all the changes taking place, the principles that have guided John's career remain remarkably consistent: stay calm, keep learning, treat people with respect, and focus on delivering meaningful outcomes.

For a man who has spent his career helping organisations transform, perhaps his greatest lesson is surprisingly simple.

Leadership isn't about being the loudest voice in the room. Sometimes it's about being the calmest.

title: Claire Singleton on Choosing Curiosity Over Comfort
html:
Not every career shift begins with a clear plan. Sometimes, it starts with a quiet, honest decision that something no longer fits.

For Claire Singleton, that moment came after years of practising as a dentist.

“By that point, I decided that it wasn't the career that I wanted to do for the rest of my life.”

There was no dramatic turning point. Just clarity—and the willingness to step away from a path that had once felt certain.

Stepping Off the Expected Path

Claire’s early career followed a structured trajectory: train, qualify, practise. It was stable, predictable, and well-defined. Walking away meant letting go of that certainty without knowing exactly what would come next. So she retrained.

That choice led her into the world of technology, where she started in middleware and debugging. The learning curve was steep, but energising. Still, something felt slightly misaligned.

It wasn’t the work—it was where she sat within it. Claire realised she was drawn less to the systems themselves and more to the people around them.

Finding Energy in People, Not Just Systems

Moving into consulting shifted everything. It brought her closer to the human side of transformation—working with teams, navigating challenges, and seeing how change played out in real environments.
That’s where her curiosity deepened.

“I think that human behaviour fascinates me.”

Not just academically, but practically. What makes someone resist change? What helps them lean in? And how do you support both?

These questions shaped her path into change management.

When Strategy Meets Reality

Working on large-scale ERP transformations, Claire saw the contrast between design and delivery. On paper, everything aligned—one system, standardised processes, shared goals.

In reality, it was far more complex. Different regions, cultures, and individuals all experienced change differently. What looked straightforward at the top often felt messy on the ground. Claire found her role in that gap—translating, listening, and guiding.

The Real Work Behind Change

For Claire, change management isn’t about ticking boxes or pushing communications. It’s about understanding people at a deeper level and meeting them where they are.

“It's actually really trying to understand what it is that's going to motivate people to come on the journey with you.”

Not everyone embraces change at the same pace. Some resist, some adapt quickly, and many sit somewhere in between. Success isn’t always full enthusiasm—sometimes it’s acceptance.
That grounded perspective shapes how she leads.

Still Led by Curiosity

What stands out in Claire’s story isn’t just the shift from one career to another. It’s the mindset behind it.

She chose curiosity over comfort. People over process. Understanding over assumption.

Even now, she reflects on what she’d study if she started again—organisational psychology. Because while systems evolve, the human side of change remains the most complex, and the most important, part.

title: Brandon Trabon on Seeing the Warning Signs Others Miss
html:
As many stories do, it started with curiosity. Not the polished, career-driven kind, but the kind that begins with a kid, a computer, and a fascination with how things work.

Where It All Began

Brandon Trabon didn’t set out to work in ERP. His journey began somewhere far more familiar and far more playful. “I was always really into video games,” he recalls. “That’s really what got me started… trying to learn how to create my own.”

By eighth grade, he was already deep in it. His family’s first computer, an expensive and almost mythical object at the time, opened a door, and he took every course he could find, chasing the idea that he could build something of his own.

But like many paths in tech, the destination didn’t quite match the starting point. “Ironically, that’s not where I ended up.”

And maybe that’s the point.

Falling Into ERP, and Finding Meaning

Brandon doesn’t romanticise his entry into ERP. “I sort of fell into it more than anything.”

What he found there was not just a career, but a pattern. About a decade into his journey, something shifted. He began noticing the subtle signals most people overlook, the early cracks in projects that, on the surface, seemed fine. “I realised that there was something wrong in the way things were done.”

It was not always obvious. Deadlines were missed but explained away, code issues pushed into “later,” and warnings softened until they disappeared.

“Before long, it’s not ‘we’ll catch up next sprint’… it’s every sprint.”

Slowly and almost invisibly, failure becomes normal.

When Failure Becomes The Norm

One project in particular stayed with him. Years later, he still talks about it. Not because it succeeded, but because it didn’t. “For all the things we did right… the delivery just completely went flat.”

The team had built something complex and even impressive, but when it came time to deliver, nothing worked. “That was like the ultimate failure.”

What made it different was not just the outcome, it was that Brandon had seen it coming. He had raised the concerns, flagged the direction, and tried to course-correct, but no one listened. That moment quietly shaped how he would show up in every project after.

Learning To See, and Speak Up

Today, Brandon sits close to the ground level of projects, the place where problems are born.

“The problem starts in things like bad code… missed deadlines… things that get excused.”

From there, he has learned something many never do, how to translate those early signals into something others can hear, not with blame or ego, but with care.

“I always try to bring it up from a standpoint of trying to be helpful.”

He has seen what happens when teams turn on each other. “It becomes nothing but fights… and then the project’s gone.”

So he leans into something simpler and harder. “You get more flies with honey than vinegar.”

It is advice passed down from his mother, and in the high-pressure world of ERP, it has become a philosophy.

The Real Work: Course Correction

Brandon’s role is not officially “project manager,” but in many ways, he is doing something just as critical. He connects the dots early, says “we’ve been here before,” and tries, gently and persistently, to shift direction before it is too late.

Sometimes people listen, corrections are made, and the project succeeds. Sometimes they don’t, and it usually ends the same way.

Still, he keeps showing up, because for Brandon, the work is not just about building software. It is about protecting the people, the effort, and the belief behind it.

title: Shireesh Mishra on Listening to Both the Data and the Instinct
html:
Sometimes the most profound insights come from the simplest questions.

A few years ago, when Shireesh Mishra was explaining his work in data and artificial intelligence to his 7-year-old son, he paused and asked something that stopped him mid-conversation:

“So, you mean you use numbers to understand people?”

He smiled at the time — but the question lingered. Because in many ways, that’s exactly what his career has been about.

A Career Built Between Logic and Intuition

With over two decades of experience across data, analytics, technology, and product management, Shireesh has spent his career at the intersection of insight and action.

Working globally across financial services, retail, and digital ecosystems, he has helped organisations turn complex data into practical decisions — but over time he has learned something that doesn’t show up in dashboards or models.

Data alone isn’t enough. Yes, data brings clarity. But intuition brings courage.

When the Numbers Said One Thing — and Instinct Said Another

One project in particular brought that lesson into sharp focus. Shireesh and his team were analysing a major marketing campaign for a retail partner, and the models were clear and consistent: every signal pointed to the same recommendation — pull back.

On paper, the decision seemed obvious. But something didn’t quite sit right.

In conversations with partners and customers, there was a different tone, and behaviour patterns hinted at something the models hadn’t fully captured.

Instead of retreating, the team made a choice that many analytics professionals find difficult — they trusted their instincts and stayed the course.

The result? The campaign turned into one of the biggest successes of the year.

Moments like that reinforce a lesson Shireesh now carries into every project:

“You use data to see patterns, but gut to sense timing. The magic happens when both speak — and you listen.”

The Human Side of Technology

Working across AI, machine learning, and advanced analytics, Shireesh is passionate about combining data-driven thinking with human judgement. Technology can reveal trends and possibilities, but people — their experience, intuition, and empathy — bring context.
Because in the end, as he puts it:

“Data can guide decisions, but people — and their instincts — still move them forward.”

Advice for Those Starting in ERP and Enterprise Technology

For newcomers stepping into ERP and enterprise systems, the scale and complexity can feel overwhelming. Shireesh understands that feeling well, and his advice is surprisingly simple: start with the business.

“Focus on understanding the business outcome first, then the system,” he says. Learn to speak both process and technology, because ERP sits at the intersection of how organisations actually work.

Success often comes from curiosity, patience, and collaboration — and perhaps most importantly, remembering that learning takes time.

“Lean on your team,” he adds. “No one masters it overnight.”

Giving Back and Lifting Others

Today, what motivates Shireesh most goes beyond the technical work. Mentorship, community service, and what he calls reverse mentoring — learning from younger colleagues and fresh perspectives — are becoming an increasingly meaningful part of his journey.

Because leadership, he believes, isn’t just about experience. It’s about staying curious, staying humble, and helping others grow along the way.

And perhaps remembering the simple question from his son that captured the heart of what this work is really about.

Sometimes the work isn’t really about the numbers. Sometimes, it’s about understanding people.

title: Mike Robinson on Chasing Success While Questioning the System
html:
What happens when the path you’ve worked hard to follow starts to feel misaligned?

For Mike Robinson, his journey has been shaped as much by reinvention as it has by ambition, unfolding across decades of experience, unexpected returns to SAP, and a growing awareness that the system he was part of didn’t always align with what he believed.

The Hustle to Get In

Mike began as a Chartered Accountant, auditing SAP clients before becoming certified in FICO, but the management consulting world never fully clicked. Instead of leaning in, he made the honest choice to step away, returning to assurance and business process work—less glamorous perhaps, but more aligned at the time.

Still, SAP had a way of finding him again. Years later, as a Risk Manager at Sovereign Insurance, he was pulled back in through a global AIA template implementation, followed by two more projects. As Mike puts it:

“SAP is not a guarantee of success, but it certainly gives you options to get ahead.”

Striving, Always

There’s a consistent thread running through Mike’s journey: a refusal to settle.

“I've always been motivated to strive towards a goal, not to accept the status quo.”

That mindset helped him break into SAP and carried him through multiple implementations—but over time, striving evolved into something more complex, because the further you go, the more clearly you begin to see the system you’re part of.

When Success Starts to Feel Uncomfortable

As his career progressed, so did his awareness. What once looked like opportunity began to reveal trade-offs, and with that came a growing discomfort. “I’ve at times felt trapped in a system that rewards the wrong behaviour… a system that’s inherently broken because its objective is profit.”

It’s not something often said out loud in our space, yet many quietly feel it—the tension between progress and purpose, between profit and people.

For Mike, it became deeply personal, shaped by experiences like redundancies packaged as “corporate progress” and decisions that didn’t sit right.

Stepping Away to Find Another Way

So he did something not everyone is willing to do—he stepped off the expected path. At one point, that meant becoming a “man in a van” for a couple of years, a stark shift from the corporate and ERP world he knew.

Now, he’s reinventing again, diving into AI, building his own consultancy, and developing vibe-coded apps—creating something that feels more aligned with both where he is and what he believes. It’s not linear, but it’s real.

Time, Pressure, and Possibility

At 56, there’s an awareness of time that comes through clearly—a sense of urgency, but also belief.

“Time is ticking but I will be rich one day soon!”

And perhaps that richness isn’t just financial—it hints at something broader: freedom, alignment, ownership, and purpose.

Paying It Forward

When asked what advice he’d give others in the ERP space, Mike keeps it simple: train, learn, get certified—then repeat.

Beneath that simplicity is a deeper truth: growth never really stops, it just changes shape. And in this current chapter, what he needs is equally human—more collaboration, new business, and people who can help bring ideas to market—because no matter how experienced you are, the next chapter is never built alone.

The Human Side of ERP

Mike’s story isn’t neat or linear—it’s layered with ambition, doubt, reinvention, and honesty. It’s about striving while questioning, stepping away and returning, holding success in one hand and uncertainty in the other.

And maybe that’s exactly why it matters—because behind every system and every project, there are humans trying to make sense of it all… and sometimes, the most powerful thing we can do is admit we’re still figuring it out.

title: Richard Williams on Staying Grounded in a Constantly Changing ERP World
html:
In an industry that’s constantly evolving, the real challenge isn’t keeping up with change—it’s staying grounded while everything around you shifts.

For Richard Williams, that grounding hasn’t come from chasing every new trend or trying to have all the answers. It’s come from experience, from staying close to the work, and from understanding that behind every system, process, and transformation… there are real people trying to make things work.

From Engineer to “Accidental” SAP Lifetimer

Richard didn’t set out to build a career in ERP. He started as an electronic engineer, but like many in the industry, his path shifted during the lead-up to Y2K—that strange, global moment of anticipation that never quite unfolded the way people expected.

What it did do, though, was open a door. Working as a maintenance planner in Taupo, New Zealand, Richard found himself stepping into SAP—and something clicked. Not just the technology, but the reality behind it.

That early grounding in maintenance stayed with him: the pressure of keeping assets running, the trade-offs, the messy, human side of operations. It shaped everything that came next.

Making ERP Practical (Not Just Perfect)

Over 25+ years, Richard has worked across industries—rail, mining, utilities, local government—and across the evolution of SAP, from ECC to S/4HANA. But through all that change, one belief has stayed constant: ERP isn’t about perfection on paper—it’s about what works in the real world.

“ERP always looks perfect on paper… until it meets the real world.”

Whether leading large transformation programs or working on mobility solutions in the field, his focus has remained the same—keeping systems grounded in how people actually work. Simple where possible. Robust where needed. Always practical.

The Moments No One Talks About

For all the experience and leadership, Richard is open about something many people don’t say out loud: confidence dips still happen. Moments of uncertainty don’t disappear with seniority—they just change shape.

And right now, with the rapid rise of AI, he sees it happening again. People questioning where they fit, whether they’re keeping up, whether they’re falling behind. His response isn’t to step back—it’s the opposite.

“Those moments aren’t a sign to step back. They’re a signal to lean in.”

Stay curious. Keep learning. Ask questions. Because growth doesn’t come from waiting for clarity—it comes from moving through uncertainty.

“The people who grow through change aren’t the ones who wait, they’re the ones who step forward.”

The Introvert Behind the Leader

What you won’t see on a CV is that Richard is naturally introverted. He enjoys collaboration and solving problems with a team, but he also knows the importance of stepping away—whether that’s a book, a bush walk, a long drive, or simply a quiet reset.

And sometimes… a side project. Like the bin reminder app he built (with a bit of humour baked in) after forgetting which bin to put out one too many times. Or experimenting with AI tools—not just professionally, but out of curiosity—giving them names along the way.

It’s a reminder that the best ideas don’t always come from being “on” all the time. Sometimes they come from stepping back.

Pressure Doesn’t Disappear — It Evolves

There’s an honesty in Richard’s story that feels important. Experience brings confidence—but it also brings expectation. More responsibility, less room for error, and a constant need to stay adaptable, especially in a world that’s changing this quickly.

And yet, his advice stays grounded: take it one piece at a time, focus on the process (not just the system), ask for help when you need it, and don’t forget to look after yourself. Because none of it works if you don’t.

If It All Disappeared Tomorrow…

If ERP vanished overnight, Richard wouldn’t rush to replace it. He’d slow down—buy a campervan, travel around Australia with his wife and dogs, and trade structured timelines for open roads. Maybe take on the occasional short-term project… just enough to keep the wine supply going.

There’s something poetic in that—a career built on structure, balance, and delivery, paired with a quiet appreciation for freedom.

Configured for Reality

If his story were a Netflix series, Richard Williams already knows what it would be called: Configured for Reality.

Because ERP will always evolve. New technologies will come. AI will keep shifting the landscape. But the real work—the work that lasts—isn’t about chasing every change.

It’s about staying grounded while everything around you shifts—understanding the people behind the process, keeping things practical when complexity creeps in, and continuing to move forward even when the path isn’t entirely clear.

Not perfect. Not polished. Just real. And in this space, that’s what makes it work.

title: Jeff Chenevey on Why It Was Never About the Technology
html:
There’s a moment that changes everything.

For Jeff Chenevey, it didn’t happen in a boardroom or during a high-stakes programme—it happened in a client office, watching a colleague take his final breath. In that moment, everything sharpened. What matters. What doesn’t. What lasts.

The Underdog Who Chose Challenge

Jeff’s story doesn’t begin with privilege or a mapped-out plan. “I came from a… lower middle class upbringing. None of my family had ever gone to college before,” he reflects.

There was no blueprint—just an underdog mindset and a quiet determination to build something more. That curiosity led him to consulting, not for status, but for challenge.

“It wasn’t about money… it was all about the challenge.”

And challenge meant stepping into the unknown—early SAP days in the US, large-scale transformations, and programmes that would shape entire organisations.

From Steel Mills to Space

Jeff’s career spans industries most people never get to touch—from steel companies in crisis, to nearly a decade transforming systems at NASA, to major programmes across government, mining, industrial manufacturing, and energy.

Each chapter brought scale, complexity, and pressure—but what stayed constant wasn’t the technology. It was the people. Even at NASA, it wasn’t just about systems—it was about connection. “You’d be going to soccer games… and NASA executives—they’re my neighbours.” Work and life blurred in the most human way, and that’s where Jeff found meaning.

The Turning Point

Then came the moment that changed everything. A colleague. A normal workday that wasn’t. “I watched this client colleague of mine… he passed away right in front of me.” That night, Jeff made a decision. “I called my wife and I said I’m done with consulting… that’s going to be me if I don’t stop doing this.”

After years of 80-hour weeks, constant travel, and relentless pressure, his priorities shifted—not his ambition, but how he defined success.

Redefining Success

Stepping away didn’t mean slowing down—it meant realigning. Jeff started his own consulting business and later became a CIO, this time with something he hadn’t had in years: balance. “I was home every night… much more balanced life.”

More importantly, it gave him space to invest in people over time—mentorship, relationships, and growth that outlast any single project. The kind of impact that doesn’t show up in deliverables, but stays with someone for decades.

The Discipline Behind the Calm

When asked how he handled pressure at places like NASA, a board, or the Pentagon, Jeff doesn’t talk about frameworks—he talks about discipline. “You have to turn away anxiety… focus on what you can control.”

For him, that meant being intentional: prioritising family, protecting time, taking care of his health, and staying grounded in purpose. Because without that discipline, he’s seen where the path leads—burnout, broken relationships, and lives that quietly unravel.

Drawing the Line

Jeff’s people-first mindset doesn’t mean tolerating everything. In a Pentagon meeting where he and his team were being dressed down, he made a different choice. “I stood up slowly… and said, ‘This meeting is now over.’”

No drama—just a boundary. Because caring about people also means respecting yourself enough to walk away when that line is crossed.

What Still Drives Him

After more than 35 years in ERP, his answer hasn’t changed. “It’s all people. It really, really is.” Whether it’s through his current startup Lumerai Advisor, mentoring students, or simply staying connected with people from decades ago, that belief continues to shape everything he does.

Because when everything else fades—the projects, the milestones, the metrics—what remains is connection.

"I don’t think about the deliverables… I think about the people.”

The Legacy He Hopes For

If you ask Jeff what he hopes people say about him, it’s not about titles or achievements. It’s something far more human.

“That I took the time to really see them.”

To see—not just the professional, but the person behind the role. Their life, their struggles, their potential. Because in the end, the real work was never just about systems—it was always about people.

title: One Year of Humans of ERP: What Fifty Conversations Taught Me About This Industry
html:
A year ago, we started something small.

Before you're an expert, you're a human. That idea became Humans of ERP: a simple experiment built around conversations with people working in enterprise technology. What began as a few interviews slowly became something much bigger than I expected. Not a media platform or a marketing campaign, but a community built around the stories we usually leave out of the industry conversation.

And if I’m honest, in the beginning, I wasn’t sure it would last.

There are already plenty of platforms in this space. Vendor blogs, conference panels, transformation success stories polished to perfection. Most are trying to sell something: a product, a framework, a version of certainty. Somewhere along the way, though, the human part gets edited out. The pressure. The doubt. The burnout. The relationships. The moments people carry long after the go-live celebrations are over.

So we tried something different. Not a vendor pitch. Not a case study. Just a conversation with the person who quietly held the project together.

Humans of ERP exists to spotlight the people shaping Australia’s ERP landscape: the consultants, architects, analysts, change leads, developers, support teams and delivery managers behind every implementation, recovery, transformation and late-night cutover. Not the version from the CV. The real version. And fifty conversations later, I think that distinction matters more than ever.

The Work Behind the Work

Across fifty interviews, one thing kept repeating itself: people wanted to talk about the things nobody had ever asked them about publicly before. The 2am cutover calls. The decisions made under impossible pressure. The mistakes they still think about years later. The colleague who carried an entire project quietly and never got mentioned in the wrap-up email.

Some conversations stayed with me long after the recording ended.

One guest spoke about finishing one of the hardest triathlons on earth at the start of December 2023, only to wake up in a Brazilian hospital bed on Boxing Day after suffering two strokes. “Strength isn’t endurance or achievement,” he said afterwards. “It’s awareness.”

A former surgical assistant spoke about spending eight years inside operating theatres, assisting with kidney transplants and tumour removals before eventually finding his way into ERP. What stayed with him across both careers was the same question: what is the actual problem we’re trying to solve here?

One consultant reflected on walking away from an eighteen-month engagement after a single day, spending nine months unemployed with less than $600 left to his name before eventually being called back for coffee by the executive who hired him. “How did you know so quickly?”

A high-performing delivery professional described burnout arriving disguised as productivity, ending in a late ADHD diagnosis that reframed an entire career built on structure and control. “How could I have missed this?”

An international student turned entrepreneur reflected on arriving in Melbourne full of ambition, watching a cryptocurrency venture collapse after a year of work, and eventually learning something simple but difficult: “The body requires maintenance.”

One senior leader shared the moment a mentee took her to lunch just to resign, and the quiet realisation that followed afterwards: “I thought I was helping. I probably didn’t listen enough.”

And one guest described a crossroads many people in this industry know intimately but rarely admit out loud — where everything looked right on paper, but nothing felt right underneath.

These aren’t edge cases. They are the texture of this industry — the part LinkedIn posts don’t quite capture.

The Gap Between Strategy and Reality

Most public conversations in enterprise technology happen at a strange altitude. We talk about transformation, strategy, roadmaps, capability uplift and digital futures, and often the bigger the language becomes, the further away it drifts from the actual work.

The conversations we had this year were the opposite: specific, grounded, sometimes uncomfortable, but always human. And I’ve come to believe that gap — between how this industry presents itself and how the work is actually experienced — is one of the biggest problems we have. Not because people are dishonest, but because polished language can slowly remove accountability from the room. The human cost disappears first. Then the lessons do too.

Seven Webinars Later, the Questions Changed

We also hosted seven webinars throughout the year across different topics, formats and rooms. At the start, the conversations sounded exactly how you’d expect. People asked about trends, frameworks, playbooks and best practice.

But something shifted around webinar four or five. The questions became sharper. People stopped asking what the trend was and started asking who owns it when it fails. They stopped asking for the playbook and started asking what happens when the playbook is wrong. The room became more honest, and once that happens, the conversation changes permanently.

That was probably the biggest surprise of Year One. A small community returning to the same conversation consistently creates more depth than any keynote ever can.

Our seventh and final webinar — our anniversary session in July — was the first one I hosted myself. For the first time, I sat on the other side of the platform we’d built. It felt unfamiliar, but it also reminded me exactly why we started this in the first place.

Taking the Community Offline

Before we close out Year One, we’re taking Humans of ERP off the screen and into the room.

Over the coming months, we’ll host a series of in-person meetups across Brisbane, Sydney, and Melbourne — bringing the Humans of ERP community together face-to-face for the first time. Smaller rooms. Better conversations. A chance to connect with the people behind the projects, stories and discussions that shaped Year One. Venues and dates are currently being finalised, with more details coming soon.

Later this year, we’ll also announce the first Humans of ERP Awards Night — recognising the people, projects and lessons that shaped the year, especially the work that usually goes unnoticed. That part feels important, because recognition in this industry often flows upward while the real weight of delivery is carried somewhere else.

To Everyone Who Was Part of Year One

If you’ve been part of Humans of ERP in any way this year — featured, interviewed, attended a webinar, shared a post, sent a message, recommended someone, or simply followed quietly from the sidelines — thank you.

This community only exists because people kept showing up for a different kind of conversation. And in an industry as noisy as ours, that’s not a small thing. It’s a meaningful one.

A Question for Year Two

I’ll leave you with this.

Think about the last project you worked on — the one that succeeded or the one that didn’t. Picture the person who quietly held it together. The one who made the difficult call, carried the assumptions nobody else challenged, stayed late when the cutover drifted sideways, and absorbed pressure so the rest of the team could keep moving.

Would they know you noticed?

That’s the question Humans of ERP exists to keep asking, and it’s the question I hope Year Two answers even better.

The ambition itself is simple: to build the biggest ERP community in the world, and build it from here in Australia — a community where talent thrives, where the work is remembered properly, and where innovation never loses its humanity.

If you want to be part of it, you already are.

— Jon Pepper

seo.title: One Year of Humans of ERP: What Fifty Conversations Taught Me About This Industry

title: Umesh Sharma on Growing Without a Plan
html:
There’s something quietly powerful about a life that doesn’t go to plan but still turns into something meaningful. 

Umesh Sharma’s story is one of those—shaped not by a clear roadmap, but by unexpected turns, steady effort, and the people who believed in him along the way.

The Path That Wasn’t Supposed to Happen

“I never had a plan to get into SAP or even IT,” Umesh shares. “I wanted to become a doctor.” 

When that path didn’t work out, he pivoted into HR and recruitment, eventually working in SAP hiring. It was there, in the middle of placing candidates and understanding their roles, that something shifted. The very people he helped into jobs began asking him why he wasn’t doing the work himself.

That question stayed with him. What started as curiosity became a decision—and eventually, a career.

“I’m kind of an accidental SAP consultant.” 

Learning by Stepping In

Umesh didn’t enter SAP with a structured plan or formal pathway. He stepped in because an opportunity opened, and he chose to take it. From there, his learning was hands-on—through documents, systems, and most importantly, the people around him who were willing to guide him.

Support became a defining part of his journey. He speaks openly about how much it mattered to have people who believed in him, especially early on. “I always had people around me who were very supportive… who kept motivating me that you can do it.” That belief helped him build his own.

Growing With the Product

Over time, Umesh found himself deeply embedded in the SuccessFactors space, particularly in Employee Central. But what stands out is how he describes that growth—not as something separate from the product, but something intertwined with it.

“The product was growing, I was growing simultaneously.” 

As the platform evolved, so did his capabilities. New features, increasing complexity, and changing expectations became part of his day-to-day. Instead of resisting that pace, he leaned into it—learning continuously and applying what he learned in real-world scenarios.

It wasn’t just about staying relevant. It was about growing alongside something that was constantly changing.

From Doing the Work to Leading People

Leadership came gradually, not as a sudden shift but as an accumulation of responsibility. When Umesh was given a bigger team, it marked a turning point in how he approached his role—not just as someone delivering outcomes, but as someone responsible for others’ growth.

He quickly realised that leadership wasn’t about control or authority. It was about creating an environment where people felt safe to speak, to make mistakes, and to learn from them. “I learned to become friend with them… even if you made a mistake, just tell me.” 

He would intentionally step back at times, allowing his team to lead conversations and handle situations on their own. It wasn’t about removing himself—it was about giving them space to grow.

And in that process, he found that leadership is never one-sided. “I felt that I also learned a lot of things from them.” 

The Human Side of Migration

Moving from India to Australia brought a different kind of challenge—one that extended beyond work. It meant adapting to a new culture, a different pace, and a new way of thinking about responsibility and ownership.

Professionally, the shift required him to move from focusing on individual tasks to understanding the full picture. Personally, it came with moments of isolation and adjustment. “When you migrate… sometimes you feel a bit depressed.” 

There were also practical challenges, like language and communication. But over time, through consistent interaction and openness, those barriers softened.

What he gained in return was perspective. He began to see the importance of building trust with stakeholders—not just delivering solutions, but helping people understand them. “Spend half an hour with them… you will see the change.”  Because in the end, success in projects often comes down to how well people are aligned.

Life Beyond the Screen

Despite working in high-pressure environments, Umesh has found simple, grounding ways to reset. He turns to yoga, excercise, and small breaks—like stepping out for a short walk or grabbing a coffee—to clear his mind.

But one of the most personal parts of his routine is his love for plants. What started as a hobby has grown into something much bigger, with dozens of plants filling his space. “I have 50–60 types of plants in my house… people say it’s a nursery.” 

For him, they’re not just decorative. They’re living things that require care, attention, and consistency—much like people. “They’re living things… somebody living along with me.” It’s a quiet reflection of how he approaches life overall.

The Advice He Carries

When asked what advice he would give to someone starting out, Umesh keeps it simple, but deeply grounded in experience.

“If you are going through hell, keep going.”

He speaks about persistence, self-belief, and the reality that growth often takes longer for some than others—but that doesn’t make it any less possible. Hard work, in his view, is non-negotiable.

At the same time, he emphasises the importance of direction and guidance. Having the right mentor—someone you trust and can be honest with—can make all the difference. It’s not about finding the most senior person, but the right person who understands your journey.

A Life That Wasn’t Planned—But Was Built

Umesh didn’t follow the path he originally imagined, but in many ways, he built something just as meaningful. His journey is shaped by resilience, curiosity, and a deep commitment to people—both in how he leads and how he grows.

It’s a reminder that not having a plan doesn’t mean you’re lost. Sometimes, it simply means you’re open to becoming something you never expected. And if you keep going, that can be more than enough.
